name: Person Rowing Boat: Medium Skin Tone
baseMeaning: Person Rowing Boat emoji. The medium skin tone modifier is applied to the figure.
tldr: 🚣🏽 Person Rowing Boat with a medium skin tone. The middle tone, often standing in for a neutral default.

contextMeanings.meaning: The gesture reads the same as the untoned version; the medium skin tone makes it the neutral version of the emoji, with almost nothing attached.
Used ironically to undercut the same reading; the tone choice is part of the joke.
In a work thread the gesture is unchanged, and the medium skin tone reads as the unremarkable version in a work thread.
Shows the same artwork as the untoned version, with the medium skin tone applied to the figure.

platformNotes.note: On iOS 🚣🏽 renders as one combined glyph with the tone applied. The medium swatch is the one several keyboards select when the picker opens, so on a device with that default set, 🚣🏽 is often the result of a finger never touching the tone list.

WhatsApp applies the medium modifier on current builds and puts the swatch in the middle of the row. It renders the most consistently of the five tones across the clients people actually use, which is part of why the medium variant is the one most often mistaken for a deliberately neutral choice.

Twemoji renders 🚣🏽 the same way on every device, which makes the medium swatch the easiest one to identify in a screenshot. The confusion is not visual: it is that a medium tone so often stands in for somebody the sender never asked you to picture.

Slack renders the medium swatch slightly flatter than the phone version, in the same way it flattens every swatch. Nothing about 🚣🏽 changes meaning in Slack, but a workspace that reacts with it constantly can make the tone look like a signature it never was.

Discord uses Twemoji and applies the modifier cleanly. The medium swatch survives copy-paste and re-posting better than the extremes of the list, which is another reason it has become the default in a lot of servers without anybody deciding on it.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z has largely stopped treating the medium swatch as neutral and uses 🚣🏽 less than the older tones, because the middle of the Fitzpatrick list no longer reads as a safe default. When it does appear it is usually an unintentional leftover.
Millennials use 🚣🏽 heavily as the neutral middle option — the tone that looks deliberate without looking like a statement. It is one of the most common swatches in messages from this cohort.
Gen X treats 🚣🏽 as a plain 🚣. The medium swatch was the default in the keyboards this cohort grew up with, so it usually reflects the settings rather than the sender.

warnings.title: Borrowed skin tones are the usual failure point
warnings.description: 🚣🏽 is frequently used to depict somebody other than its sender, and because it is treated as the neutral pick, it is the tone most likely to be used to refer to somebody other than the sender. When the person being depicted is in the room, the tone is read as a description of them.

seoTitle: 🚣🏽 Person Rowing Boat Medium Skin Tone Emoji Meaning - What Does 🚣🏽 Mean?
seoDescription: What does the person rowing boat emoji 🚣🏽 mean? Person Rowing Boat showing a figure seated in a narrow boat, one oar pulled through the water. Covers the medium skin tone variant, the misread it invites, and how to reply.

longForm.overview:
There are five skin tones in the Fitzpatrick set and 🚣🏽 is the one in the middle of them — Person Rowing Boat with a medium skin tone, a figure seated in a narrow boat, one oar pulled through the water. Because it sits in the middle of the list and several keyboards default to it, it is the variant that most often ends up standing in for "somebody", with no view at all from the sender. Often the choice of someone who is not using skin tone to make a point, which is why it reads as the neutral stand-in

That neutrality is useful and it is also the reason to be careful. 🚣🏽 reads as rowing, keeping pace, or working through something slowly, the same job 🚣 does. But because the medium swatch is so often pressed by people who are simply not thinking about skin tone, it is also the variant that most often ends up describing somebody who is not the sender — and the most likely to be misread that way.

The situations it turns up in are the family ones, unchanged by the tone. It gets mixed up with 🛶 Canoe more than it should — the canoe is an empty vessel for leisure, the rowboat always shows a person putting in the work. The misread that comes up most often with this glyph is specific enough to name: it gets assumed to be a quiet boating scene when it is usually about effort — the long stroke suggests grinding through something at a steady pace.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The gesture is the same one 🚣 makes, so the family habits carry straight over. What changes with 🚣🏽 is who tends to send it and what they are assuming about the reader.

The medium swatch is the workhorse of the set. 🚣🏽 is the one people send when they are not trying to make a point about skin tone at all, which makes it the variant most likely to be used as a stand-in for someone unspecified. You will see it in saying you are working through a slow week, and in keeping pace with a long task, and in a great many places where the sender simply pressed the emoji that was already selected.

The flip side of that ubiquity is that the tone carries almost no signal of its own. 🚣🏽 reads as the neutral version of the emoji, with almost nothing attached, and it tends to disappear into the line it sits on. If the sender wanted the skin tone to mean something, this is the variant that will not deliver it.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
The family rule applies first, and it is the one spelled out above: the standard misread of this glyph belongs to 🚣 itself, and every tone in this family inherits it.

The trap for 🚣🏽 is that its neutrality is an illusion. It is chosen by reflex more often than by intent, and a reflex choice is not a statement about the sender. Do not send 🚣🏽 expecting it to be read as "this is what I look like" unless that is genuinely why you picked it — the medium swatch is the one most likely to have been selected without a thought at all.

And skip it when a specific person is being depicted and you would be guessing at their skin tone. The default-position argument cuts the other way here: the easiest swatch to press is the easiest one to press by accident, and it is the one that looks most like a decision.
longForm.howToReply:
The simplest reply is 🚣 with the same gesture and no tone commentary, because the medium swatch does not usually carry a message of its own.

If the sender was representing themselves, though, 🏽 back is warmer than 🚣 — it says you registered what they chose. If they were representing somebody else, match the gesture only.

faqs.question: What does 🚣🏽 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🚣🏽 is Person Rowing Boat with a medium skin tone. The gesture reads as rowing, keeping pace, or working through something slowly.

faqs.question: Is the medium skin tone in 🚣🏽 a statement?
faqs.answer: Rarely on its own. It is the middle swatch in the tone list, and the one several keyboards land on by default when the tone picker opens. It is the variant people pick when they are not thinking about skin tone, so it rarely reads as one.

faqs.question: What does 🚣🏽 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: The tone does not change the gesture, so the read is the same. There is no separate gendered reading of 🚣.

faqs.question: Is 🚣🏽 rude?
faqs.answer: Not because of the swatch. The gesture carries that risk on its own, and the medium tone does not add to it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🚣🏽 and 🚣?
faqs.answer: The swatch, and only the swatch. 🚣 is the tone-less version and is the safer choice whenever you are not depicting a specific person.
